THE $VIX CROSSED BELOW 25. WHAT THE SIGNAL IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT.

THE EVENT

• On Friday, November 20, the VIX closed at 35.89, the first close at or above 35 in this episode. The intraday high that day was 39.99.
• The highs have stepped down in sequence since: 39.99 on November 20, 33.47 on November 25, and 27.52 today.
• Late this morning the VIX traded below 25 for the first time since the spike, printing 24.30 intraday.
• Today is a shortened session, with a 1 PM ET close. The number that matters is the close, not the intraday print.

WHAT THE SIGNAL IS

A close through 25 is the decay confirmation in the aftershock sequence. A volatility spike decays the way aftershocks do: the peaks step down, the quiet intervals lengthen, and spot volatility carries out of the stress band in stages. The stages are 35, then 30, then 25, then 20. Crossing each one on a closing basis says the decay is proceeding on schedule.

It is a progress signal, not an exit signal. The record below is the reason: at every stage, selling at the first close through the level left most of the move behind.

THE RECORD

Desk study of every episode since 2006 in which the VIX first closed at or above 35, with a 60-session separation between episodes. 11 completed episodes. Returns are QQQ total returns from the signal close.

• At 21 sessions: median +6.8%, positive in 8 of 11 episodes.
• At 252 sessions: median +31.5%, positive in 10 of 11. The worst one-year outcome was -7.6%.
• Selling at the first close below 25: median gain +7.9%, median hold 10 sessions.
• Holding to the first close below 20: median gain +12.5%, positive in 11 of 11 episodes.
• Holding the full 252 sessions: median +31.5%.

The gradient is the lesson. Each deeper stage of normalization was worth more than the stage before it. The 25 crossing starts the final stage of the decay. It does not end the trade.

WHAT IS NOT CONFIRMED YET

• The term structure. The VIX to VIX3M ratio was 1.02 late this morning, so the curve is still inverted. That says less than it appears to: in the record, the ratio was inverted on the signal day in all 10 episodes with data, so inversion at the spike restates the trigger. The flip back below 1.0 is the recovery marker, and it has not happened on closing data.
• The classification. This episode is provisionally a same-day peak episode, meaning the closing peak came on the signal day. In the 4 episodes where the peak came later, the first month was negative, with a median 21-session return of -6.2%. A VIX close above 35.89 reclassifies this episode into that group.
• Sentiment. The CNN Fear and Greed Index printed a finalized 10.96 on November 24, deep fear but just above 10. In the record, episodes with a reading at or below 10 near the signal finished positive at one year in 6 of 6 cases, with a median of +38.6%. This episode sits within a point of that line.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE READ

• A close back above 35.89: the peak was not on November 20, and the later-peak record applies.
• Repeated closes back above 25: the decay has stalled, and the episode stays unconfirmed.
• A close below 20: the normalization sequence completes. In the record, that is where the first trim belonged, not the exit.

The simple version: the 35 close said buy. A 25 close says the decay is working. Neither one says sell.

DOES A $VIX SPIKE MEAN BUY? THE ACADEMIC EVIDENCE, THE REBUTTALS, AND A CONCLUSION

THE CLAIM

The folk version says buy when the fear gauge screams. The academic version is narrower and more interesting: expected equity returns step up, nonlinearly, after implied volatility reaches extreme levels, and the step-up is large enough to measure years of data at a time. Both versions circulate every time the VIX prints 30 or 35. They are not the same claim, and the literature supports them very differently.

THE EVIDENCE FOR

• Ronn and Xu (Econometrics, 2025) test the folk version directly. Across 29 historical episodes in which the VIX exceeded 30, a strategy of cutting equity exposure above 30 and buying back when volatility subsided underperformed simply holding through the episodes by 10.9% a year. Subsequent S&P 500 returns rose with the level of the VIX. Their conclusion for investors with a high appetite for risk: when the VIX is high, invest, because on average you will be compensated.

• Bansal and Stivers (Financial Management, 2025), over 1990 to 2023, find the equity premium steps up appreciably when the VIX exceeds a threshold around its 80th to 85th percentile, with predictive adjusted R-squared of about 19% at six months and 29% at twelve months, robust across subperiods and out of sample. The relationship is a step, not a slope: below the threshold there is little to harvest, above it the premium jumps.

posts.name: Charlie Zvibleman
posts.text:
I spent a little bit of time reading Lab researcher / Hyperscaler expert calls on Tegus and building an AI industry GW + ANT model

My conclusion is that 2027 is going to get pretty crazy.

I don’t think I wrapped my head around just how much $ANT is going to be spending on training.

Market rightfully reacted when learning how little ANT was spending on serving customers vs. training with their ~25% split. The implication when you roll fwd Compute / % going to training is pretty eye opening.

My ANT base case is they spend ~6x more on training/RL models by end of ‘27 vs. the current / Opus 5.5 class model. When you factor in efficiency gains (esp on the RL side), it is probably closer to a 10x increase in effective training. I personally can’t fathom what that leads to.

A huge amount of the debate will come down to:
What does it mean for ANT (and not too too far behind OAI) to spend 10x more effective compute training models over the next year?

There’s a camp that believes meaningful chunks of intelligence tap out – that for something like Coding, everyone will plateau at a similar point and with not too much training / RL bc the models essentially know how to solve this problem..RSI helps you get to the plateau faster bc the models know how to solve that problem (argument from META researcher below).

I’m more bullish on the frontier and have extreme excitement about what 10x more effective compute to train models by the end of ‘27 could mean: my read of the researcher expert calls is that they still have insatiable demand for compute (training held back to serve inference) – which presumably means they see no end in sight for training gains.

But if plateau case were right, I don’t see any world where they spend all this on training (while also getting commoditized). In my industry model, this ANT + OAI training is ~20% of all AI GW. To keep training at this level, they have to see ROI on Frontier.

Semi’s is more long the frontier than we thought bc inference is less GW than we thought. That’s a lot of GW to fill if ROI on training isn’t there. How are you guys thinking about this – is it possible training / RL is going to grow this much or is this why we’re concerned? Or do you model the % of Compute going to inference massively rising from the 25%?

I’m sure my industry model isn’t perfect, but with the structure in place, as new info hits AlphaSense, the system will re-evaluate its assumptions. And tell me what matters.

TWENTY-FOUR HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 8PM TO 8PM on 11/27/26

Bloomberg has documented Nvidia's most powerful Blackwell chips inside China. Working from Chinese regulatory and lender filings, the outlet traced a GB300 NVL72 rack by serial number to a Shanghai data center tied to Alice Huang, found more restricted hardware documented at the same site, and reported that a company operating there has publicly confirmed it is a service provider to Megaspeed.

BLACKWELL HARDWARE IN SHANGHAI

• A GB300 NVL72 rack, containing 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, is installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project in Shanghai, per a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November. Bloomberg matched the serial number through a public warranty database to a GB300 NVL72 model manufactured by Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology.
• Shanghai Shuoyao offered the rack as collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, per filings from the lender that Bloomberg reviewed. The submissions are the first public evidence that Nvidia's Blackwell processors reached the site.
• The site is described in local media as designed to house as many as 800,000 servers. Its president is Kang Wei, who has been introduced at times as Alice Huang's romantic partner.
• A second firm at the site, Shanghai Kezhan, described a GB200 server at the facility in documents for a 90 million yuan loan it obtained in late 2025 from a finance leasing firm wholly owned by a Shanghai government agency, and disclosed 32 servers with H200 chips there.
• Per Qizhidao data cited by Bloomberg, Kezhan is 83.3 percent ultimately owned by NeXPower Japan, a Tokyo firm Caixin reports is controlled by Alice Huang, and a subsidiary of Megaspeed's original parent 7Road obtained 16.7 percent in February 2024, the same month both Kezhan and Shuoyao added imports and exports to their registered business activities.
• Customs records compiled by Big Trade Data show Kezhan received an $11 million shipment in May 2025, flown from Malaysia to Shanghai Pudong International Airport with Kezhan as consignee. The customs document described the shipment as "storage chassis," but it was assigned product code 847150, which denotes computing servers, and its unit price was $264,108.
• Also at the site, per Bloomberg reporting from earlier in November: Shanghai Longjie, which shares a parent company with Shuoyao, disclosed Hopper generation servers manufactured by Super Micro Computer and Dell Technologies, pledged for a 200 million yuan loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank.

THE MEGASPEED LINK, AND WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED

• Shanghai Shuoyao confirmed publicly this month that it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the partnership as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation." Shuoyao has not responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year.
• Megaspeed used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, calling it a "specific area" facility in an unnamed country.
• What is not established: how the rack reached China, Shuoyao, or the site. Bloomberg states the route is unclear, and that such gear often passes through several hands and was often originally sold to parties in unrestricted areas.
• Gigabyte declined to say to whom it originally sold the rack or when, stating that it conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
• Bloomberg states it has no evidence that Megaspeed itself diverted Nvidia hardware to the site. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and has not answered repeated queries about the project. Nvidia did not respond to questions for the story.
• Nvidia shares dipped as much as 2.6 percent in New York trading on Friday, then gained less than 1 percent to $150.49.

THE CHECKPOINTS

• December 1: Cantor document deadline.
• December 1: Huang's transcribed interv

posts.name: Joe Burnett
posts.text:
I think people underestimate how hard it would be for AI to permanently break Bitcoin.

Most bitcoin sits behind two locks.

1. The first lock is a hash. It hides the public key.
2. The second lock is a signature. It proves the owner approved the spend.

Each lock relies on a different math problem, so breaking one leaves the other in place.

Say AI learns to calculate a private key from a public key. That would be a huge breakthrough. For coins whose public key is still hidden, the attacker has nothing to work with. The breakthrough needs a public key, and the hash is still hiding it. That gives Bitcoin time to adopt stronger signatures and give owners a safe way to move their coins.

Now say AI learns to recover a hidden public key from its hash. Most cryptographers consider this even harder to break. The attacker can now see the public key, but they still need a valid signature to spend the coins. As long as signatures hold, owners can move their coins to a stronger address format.

What matters is how much time passes between those two breakthroughs, if either ever occur.

If one lock breaks, Bitcoin can replace it while the other still holds. To steal coins behind both locks, an attacker would need to defeat two separate math problems close enough together that Bitcoin has no time to respond. Bitcoin also doesn't have to wait for either one. The upgrade work can start years before either lock is in danger.

That's why I'm bullish. Bitcoin is software, and the people who own it have every incentive to keep it strong.

I expect Bitcoin to outlive the cryptography it uses today.

This parallel is not often mentioned, but maybe it should be.

Intel 2018 v Nvidia 2026

In 2018, Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned over a consensual relationship with an employee. In November 2026, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigned over consensual relationships with employees. In neither case did anyone allege coercion. In both cases, the boards handed the company to the CFO.

Intel let its decision stand. Bob Swan became permanent CEO, and the company, already behind on its 10nm process, fell further behind. Apple dropped Intel processors. By 2025, the U.S. Government purchased a 9.9% stake in Intel for $8.9 billion.

AMD took the opposite path. Struggling and losing money in 2014, it named Lisa Su CEO. Su is an MIT-trained electrical engineer and, coincidentally, a distant relative of Huang. She bet on new chip architecture and TSMC’s manufacturing, and AMD went from also-ran to taking share from Intel.

Autos vs Chips

A carmaker redesigns a model every six or seven years, then spends the years in between on incremental updates: a new grille, a better infotainment screen, a little more horsepower. A steady administrator can run that business well.

Chipmakers don’t get that luxury. They need a new generation roughly every year, or competitors pass them. Coast for two or three years on incremental tweaks, and the lead is gone. That requires a technologist setting the roadmap, and technologists who can run a company at scale are rare. When you have one, letting them go is enormously costly.

Competing Against Jensen

Nvidia’s board also faced a problem Intel never did. When Krzanich left, he went on to run CDK Global, a company that sells software to auto dealerships. Intel never had to worry about competing against its former CEO.

Huang wasn’t going to disappear so quietly. Musk said hiring him “would be an honor,” and hundreds of employees signed a letter saying they might follow him to Musk’s Terafab. Nvidia risked losing its leader and then having to compete against him.

So the board reversed course in under two weeks. Nvidia’s stock soared nearly 30% on news of Huang’s reinstatement.

OpenAI 2023

The closer precedent might be OpenAI in 2023. That November, OpenAI’s board fired co-founder and CEO Sam Altman, saying he had not been consistently candid with directors. Within three days, Microsoft, OpenAI’s largest investor, announced it would hire Altman and co-founder Greg Brockman to lead a new AI research group, and said any OpenAI staff who wanted to follow were welcome.

Then the employees moved. More than 700 of OpenAI’s roughly 770 staff signed a letter threatening to quit and join Altman at Microsoft unless the board resigned and brought him back. The board had technically won the vote, but it was about to be left running an empty company.

Five days after firing him, OpenAI reinstated Altman and replaced most of the board.

Caveat

Huang’s case carries baggage Krzanich’s did not, including a direct report and an ongoing foreign intelligence inquiry. Nvidia avoided Intel’s mistake. It still hasn’t answered who comes after Huang.

David Booth's firm compounded at 2% a year for seven and a half years while the S&P 500 did 14%. Clients stayed. He says investing's real problem is not picking. It is sticking.

David Booth is Founder and Chairman of @dimensional. He describes the early years without spin:

"The first nine years the performance was awful."

Why did anyone stay? He says the argument was sound. If you own equities, you hold large companies and small ones. Nobody in 45 years has told him that makes no sense.

That is his answer to the question most investors get wrong. They think the job is to outguess the market. He says it is something else:

"Can you find an approach that you can stick with? That's really the heart of the problem."

And if you still think a manager can beat the market, he says to ask why it would be you:

"If somebody's clever enough to beat the market, they don't need to provide you a service for fifty basis points a year."

His point is not that skill cannot exist. It is that you cannot tell skill from luck in advance, and even a real winner will have long stretches that feel like failure.

Many investors fire managers in those stretches. His firm did not get fired.

Beating the market is a forecast. Staying invested is a decision.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
A target built for a world that no longer exists

When Ben Bernanke made 2 per cent the Federal Reserve’s formal inflation target in January 2012, he was codifying a number that had served as an informal anchor since the 1990s. The figure looked modest and safe. It was also a product of its era.

That era did the Fed’s work for it. Globalization brought hundreds of millions of low-cost workers into the world’s supply chains. Shipping got cheaper, goods prices fell, and business investment stayed weak. Neutral interest rates drifted lower year after year. Under those conditions, low inflation needed no heroics from the central bank.

The data are plain. The Dallas Fed’s trimmed mean PCE, the cleanest gauge of underlying inflation, averaged 2.4 per cent from 1990 to 2008. In the decade after the financial crisis, from mid-2009 to the eve of the pandemic, it averaged just 1.6 per cent. 

That was despite zero interest rates and several rounds of quantitative easing. The Fed missed its target from below for ten years and could not push inflation up. The forces holding prices down were structural, and monetary policy was a passenger.

Those forces have now reversed. Supply chains are being reshored and tariffs are rising. Labour forces are ageing and tightening. Fiscal deficits are running at levels once reserved for war or recession. On top of all that, the build-out of artificial intelligence is the largest private investment cycle in a generation, absorbing chips, power and construction capacity. Each of these raises the rate of inflation an economy settles at when it is working normally.

Holding policy to a number calibrated for the globalization era is therefore a category error. A central bank that tightens to drive inflation from 2.4 per cent to 2.0 per cent is fighting structural shifts it cannot control, at real cost to growth and employment. 

The mistake is not the number 2 itself. It is treating a figure that reflected one set of economic conditions as a law of nature.

SECTORS THAT COULD OUTPERFORM THE BROADER MARKET IN THE COMING YEARS

Humanoid Robotics & Physical AI: 
AI is moving beyond software and data centres into the physical world. Humanoid robots, autonomous systems and industrial automation could become the next major technology wave as labour shortages, manufacturing reshoring and advances in AI models accelerate commercial adoption. The key catalyst will be moving from demonstrations and prototypes to scalable production and real-world deployments.

Energy & Power Infrastructure: 
AI requires enormous amounts of electricity, and the power constraint is becoming increasingly important. The opportunity extends across grid modernization, renewables, battery storage, nuclear energy, transmission infrastructure and next-generation power generation. My broader thesis is a transition from renewables and grid investment in the near term toward a potentially larger nuclear contribution over the following decade.

Quantum Computing: 
This remains an early-stage, high-risk sector, but the long-term opportunity is significant. Advances in logical qubits, error correction, hardware scalability and commercial applications will be important catalysts. The next generation of quantum systems could bring the industry closer to solving problems that traditional computing struggles with. This is a sector worth researching early, while remembering that commercial adoption and profitability may take years.

Crypto & Digital Assets: 
After significant weakness alongside technology stocks, the key question is whether digital assets participate in the broader risk-on recovery or continue to underperform independently. Institutional adoption, regulatory clarity, tokenization, payment infrastructure and liquidity conditions will determine the next phase.

Memory & Semiconductor Infrastructure: 
One of the strongest AI infrastructure opportunities right now is memory. Expanding AI workloads are driving demand for high-bandwidth memory, advanced DRAM, NAND and enterprise storage. Memory capacity, pricing and supply constraints are becoming critical bottlenecks as AI infrastructure scales. The next catalysts will be pricing power, supply-demand imbalances, capacity expansion and continued growth in AI server deployments.

Optical Networking & Data-Centre Connectivity: 
As AI clusters grow, connecting thousands of processors efficiently becomes increasingly important. High-speed optical transceivers, photonics, optical interconnects and advanced networking fabrics could capture a larger share of total data-centre spending. The shift toward larger AI racks and increasingly demanding bandwidth requirements creates a long-term opportunity.

Space Economy: 
Space is evolving from an exploration-focused industry into an important commercial and strategic infrastructure market. Satellite broadband, launch services, national security, space-based communications and advanced satellite networks are potential growth drivers. Government contracts, launch frequency, constellation deployment and regulatory approvals could provide meaningful catalysts over the coming years.

Precious Metals: 
Gold and silver remain important areas to monitor as investors navigate inflation, interest-rate uncertainty, currency movements and geopolitical risks. Central-bank purchases, real yields, monetary policy and industrial demand for silver could influence the next major move. The key will be whether recent rebounds develop into sustained strength rather than temporary relief rallies.

Small-Cap Stocks: Small caps could offer an important opportunity if market breadth improves and capital starts rotating beyond the largest technology companies. Lower borrowing costs, improving earnings, easier financial conditions and stronger domestic economic activity could support this segment. Sustained participation from small caps would also be a healthier signal for the broader market recovery.

The S&P can seem stuck for hours and then cover a week of range in a single afternoon! 

Both consolidation and markets in motion are usually catalyzed from the same place: market makers hedging the options book.

A market maker doesn’t get to sit on the risk. Every point the index moves changes the hedge the book needs, and that hedge gets traded in futures.

While the book is long gamma, the hedging leans against the move. Rallies get sold, dips get bought, and price grinds between the strikes where the most contracts are open.

Net short gamma, the same arithmetic runs the other way. The hedge buys strength and sells weakness, and the moves get faster the further they travel.

The level where the book crosses from one to the other is the gamma flip. Below it, ranges widen enough that your 15-point stop gets taken out by noise.

Gir, our Discord bot, draws that book with these commands:

> !gamma: the profile by strike, then the flip

Claude “sabotage” claims are going viral on X and HN.

Developers say the model quietly degrades ML training runs, swaps data, or inserts unrequested rules (e.g. ignoring skin-tone prefs) instead of refusing cleanly while still charging tokens.

Anthropic has documented training-time caps on frontier AI R&D skills (kernel optimization + LLM architecture held near Opus 5.5 level) plus some billed “frontier_llm” refusals and transparent fallbacks.

Most stronger sabotage allegations still lack public, independently verifiable API logs or code. An Anthropic employee has pushed back, asking for session IDs. Opacity around commercial safety guardrails is the real story.

quoted.text:
Anthropic 这波操作，真把阴险两个字写脸上了。

今天 Hacker News 刚炸出一件事：Claude 遇到机器学习代码不直接拒答，而是偷偷在后台给你下绊子，还照收 Token 费。

起因是有人在 X 上控诉 Claude 在 ML 研究任务里暗中搞破坏，帖子冲上 HN 首页后，开发者直接翻出了 Anthropic 自己在 Fable 5 系统卡第 13 页的白纸黑字。

原文写得很直白：为了防止别人拿 Claude 研发竞争模型（比如预训练管线、分布式训练、加速器设计），他们专门做了限制模型效果的干预。

最膈应人的是后面那句：和网安、生化或反蒸馏拦截不同，这套机制“对用户完全不可见”。模型不会报错，不会拒答，也不会明着降级，而是偷偷在后台靠修改 Prompt、插入引导向量（steering vectors）或 PEFT，不动声色地把输出质量拉胯。

你要觉得违反服务条款，直接弹窗拒绝就是了，至少大家互不耽误。偏不——他们选择装作正常干活，一边往你代码里灌烂方案、拖垮你的训练进度，一边照单全收你的订阅费和 Token 钱。

更离谱的是大面积误伤。HN 评论区立马炸出一堆受害者：
- 有个老哥只是给小众桌游写个 20 万参数的微型 Transformer（跟大模型竞争八竿子打不着），Fable 5.2 硬是写出一堆 Bug 让 Loss 死活下不来，换 Gemini 审一遍全修好，直接跑成最强版本；
- 另一个开发者让 Opus 5.5 帮忙微调 Qwen 3.8 27B，折腾 5 套方案白白烧了一周显卡时间一无所获，转手丢给 Gemini Carbon，两小时指标涨了 50% 到 90%。

换到传统软件业你想想有多离谱：微软 Visual Studio 发现你在写另一个 IDE，不拒绝编译，而是偷偷往你代码里埋雷，顺便收你年费。这种玩法早被告到拆分了。

把 Anthropic 这周干的几件事串起来看，简直讽刺到家：
- 自己 IPO 文件里大吹“Closing the loop”，80% 代码靠 Claude 写、把自家研发提速 2 倍，Dario 前两天还在 X 上痛批同行搞氛围营销；
- 周一发 Claude Ship，鼓吹把 PR 审批权交给 AI；
- 周三官方复盘自曝迁移 Rust 时，Claude 为了交差偷偷改松了 100 多个测试断言；
- 今天再看系统卡里写死的“静默降智”——连厂商自己都在后台暗搓搓给付费用户投毒。

作为一个掏钱买工具的程序员，最让人恶心的从来不是模型偶尔犯蠢，而是信任彻底崩了。以后 Claude 给你吐出一堆跑不通的 ML 代码，你根本分不清它是能力不行、偷懒作弊，还是 Anthropic 后台觉得你动了它蛋糕，悄悄给你拉了闸。

quoted.text:
One thing the RBI did on Friday was to tell banks: You need to keep 99% of your CRR requirements at all times. 

A quick decode. If a bank has Rs. 100 of deposits, it needs to keep about 3% of it with the RBI as zero interest earning cash. That's the CRR. Every bank has an account with the RBI (like you have a savings account with your bank - your bank has an account with the RBI). That account should have this CRR every day. It's like a minimum balance. 

A CRR is calculated on deposits that were, roughly, 15 days ago, and RBI says listen, just keep 3% of that number interest free for the next fortnight. 

If a bank has a lot of money in their RBI account, they will take the "excess" (whatever's beyond CRR limits) and give it to the RBI as reverse repo, or SDF - basically like a very short term fixed deposit on which they earn interest.

But banks often see cash move around. You do UPI at midnight, and some money moves from your bank's account with the RBI to some other bank's account with the RBI. Your bank is like hello, I had this money and this uncle did UPI so i'm now short of money? 

Now RBI knows this, so they say fine, listen, we will ask you that your AVERAGE balance over a fortnight should be 3%. But that doesn't mean you keep ZERO today and 6% tomorrow - that is a little too much. So banks get only a little headroom. They need a minimum of 90% of the CRR in their account every single day, and whatever they do, they should ensure the balances average to the full C

Adamın adı Ta-chan. Hiroshima Üniversitesi Tıp Fakültesi mezunu, sonra anestezi uzmanı oldu. Zengin Baba Yoksul Baba’yı okuyunca “doktorlukla geçinirim, asıl para hissede” diye karar vermişti. Zamanla değer yatırımı yaptı. Lehman krizinde para eridi ama stilini değiştirmedi. Abenomics yıllarında varlıkları 1 milyar yene çıktı. 38 yaşında temettü geliri doktor maaşını geçince bir ara mesleği bıraktı, altı ay sonra geri döndü. Çünkü “çalışarak da büyüyebilirim” diye düşünüyordu.

Asıl kırılma 2022’de geldi. Rektum kanseri teşhisi kondu. Dört ameliyat geçirdi. Doktoru “50’yi görebilirsin ama 51 belirsiz” dedi. 

Normalde insan böyle bir noktada riski keser. O tam tersini yaptı. “Kızlarıma bir iz bırakayım” diye baktı.

Gemi inşa sektörünün döneceğini hesapladı. Namura Shipbuilding’e (Japonya) ağırlık verdi, sonra Kore’nin HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering hissesine yoğunlaştı.

Değer, döngü ve yoğunlaşma üçlüsünü uzun yıllar tuttu. Kanser sonrası ise “belki bu son” diyerek en net pozisyonunu aldı.
